utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the great English novels.
I'm your host, and over this series we're working through Dickens's extraordinary, infuriating, deeply humane masterpiece.
A novel about the law, about fog, about what institutions do to human beings — and about the stubborn persistence of love inside all of that.
Today we're opening with the novel's very first pages — Dickens's famous fog, and what it announces about everything that follows.
To help us, I have three wonderful guests.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and few novels repay that reading more richly than this one.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — someone who can tell us exactly what the Court of Chancery was, and precisely why it was so destructive.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read Bleak House more times than perhaps any person should admit to — and loves it more each time.
James, let's start with you — because the novel opens, famously, not with a character or a plot, but with weather.
What is Dickens doing in those first extraordinary paragraphs?
What he's doing is something quite audacious for the opening of a novel — he refuses to give you a person, or a story.
He gives you an environment, and he insists that the environment is the argument.
The fog and mud are not backdrop — they are the condition of life in this city, in this legal system, in this novel.
And then he does something wonderfully strange.

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
A dinosaur on Holborn Hill.
It's a joke, but it's a serious joke — this city is so primordial, so buried under accumulated filth, that geological time feels plausible.
And the word 'accumulating at compound interest' arrives a few lines later — suddenly the mud is financial.
What stops me every time is that phrase — 'gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun.'
"Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown snowflakes — gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun."
The sun hasn't set — it has died.
That's a very different thing, and Dickens knows exactly the difference he's making.
We're not in a temporary night — we're in a world where light itself may be finished.
And that registers in the body when you read it — there's a real chill to it.
Both of those observations are exactly right — and I want to push them a little further.
Notice who is in this fog — foot passengers losing their footing, jostling each other in 'a general infection of ill temper.'
These are ordinary people, urban poor, doing what the city requires them to do — and the city punishes them for it.
The mud accumulates 'at compound interest' — James noticed the financial language — but compound interest punishes the people who have least.
The fog isn't neutral — it is the atmosphere that the powerful generate, and the powerless must breathe.
Daniel is right about the asymmetry — and it connects directly to the Court of Chancery, which Dickens introduces almost immediately after.
Chancery was not an abstract evil — it was a real institution that could hold an estate in litigation for decades while the people connected to it were slowly destroyed.
By the time we reach chapter twenty-four, Dickens has a character speak those consequences with devastating precision.
"Of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits and hopes, of all the living and the dead world, this one poor soul alone comes natural to me, and I am fit for.
There is a tie of many suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on earth that Chancery has not broken!"
'The only tie Chancery has not broken.' That sentence lands like a verdict.
Chancery doesn't just slow things down — it severs the human connections that make life liveable.
And notice the rhetorical structure of that passage — 'of all... of all... of all' — three times the phrase accumulates before the blow falls.
It's almost biblical in its rhythm — and that's deliberate.
Dickens is reaching for the register of lamentation — this is a formal mourning for a life that the law has eaten.
Which takes us back to James's opening fog — 'gone into mourning for the death of the sun.'
Mourning is structural in this novel — it's built into the weather.
What I find remarkable is that the novel holds its critique of institutions alongside something almost unbearably tender.
There's a moment late in the novel — Sir Leicester Dedlock, aristocrat, establishment figure — who has just had his world destroyed by scandal.
And he insists on being read by his own code — listen to this.
"I assert no cause whatever of complaint against her. That I have ever had the strongest affection for her, and that I retain it undiminished."
Dickens doesn't let Sir Leicester off the hook for what he represents — but he insists the man is also capable of that.
The novel is too honest, and too humane, to reduce anyone entirely to their function in the system.
That tension — between the system's cruelty and individual human dignity — feels like it's at the very heart of what we'll be exploring.
We've had fog, mud, Chancery, and a dinosaur on Holborn Hill — and we're only at the opening.
In our next segment, we'll go deeper into Chancery itself — the machine at the novel's centre — and what Dickens understood about how it worked on people.

segments.title: The Machinery of Injustice: Social Critique and Jo's World

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart — chapter by chapter, character by character, passage by passage.
I'm your host, and today we're deep in Chapter Eleven — and just into Twelve — where the novel's social critique arrives at full force.
We're looking at Jo — the crossing-sweeper, one of the most heartbreaking figures in all of Victorian fiction — and at the grotesque comedy of a political class that cannot see him at all.
Three guests are with me today, and I want to introduce them properly.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — every institution in the text is, for him, a mechanism that protects the wealthy and grinds down the poor.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — the person who can tell you what these institutions actually were, how the law worked, and what destitution truly meant in this period.

And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and cares fiercely about what it feels like to read — the music of a sentence, the moment that makes you put the book down and breathe.
We begin with the inquest into the death of the mysterious Nemo, and Dickens's masterly cut between the circus of testimony and the quiet grief of a boy with a broom.
The moment I always come back to in this chapter is Mrs. Piper at the inquest.
Dickens is doing something wickedly clever with her testimony — it's almost entirely parentheses, almost entirely punctuation-free, and it tells us almost nothing useful.
The narrator sets it up perfectly:
"Why, Mrs. Piper has a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
That contrast — a great deal to say, not much to tell — is the whole comedy of official testimony, isn't it?
And then there's this extraordinary detail — she insists on calling the dead man "the plaintive."
She's borrowed a legal term — the plaintiff — garbled it, and applied it to a corpse.
The law has already consumed the man's identity before he's even buried.
That malapropism is doing more work than it might seem.
Mrs. Piper has absorbed the vocabulary of legal process — but only the surface of it, the sound without the sense.
Which is precisely what the inquest offers everyone present: the form of justice without its substance.
And look at what she actually reports — rumour, dream, hearsay.
She dreamed he might take a pickaxe to a child's head — and Dickens makes this comic, which is the brilliant trap he sets for us.
We laugh at Mrs. Piper, and in laughing we become complicit in the system that dismisses the dead man with exactly this quality of attention.
He is reduced to rumour — to a man who was reported to have sold himself, whatever that means — and the court accepts it.
The coroner's inquest in this period was genuinely the primary mechanism for investigating unexplained deaths among the poor.
And the quality of testimony Dickens depicts is not especially satirical — it's actually fairly accurate.
Neighbourhood witnesses routinely gave evidence of this character: impressions, fears, rumours, third-hand reports.
What Dickens adds is the comedy of the syntax — that extraordinary run-on sentence about Alexander James Piper, eighteen months old, whose teething troubles somehow become admissible evidence.
The point is that the institution exists, it functions, it produces verdicts — but it cannot see the actual person at the centre of it.
And yet there is someone in this chapter who does see Nemo — who knew him, who received genuine kindness from him.
Jo gives his testimony, and it's the most devastating passage in these chapters.
That passage about Jo's testimony — I find it almost unbearable to read, in the best possible sense.
Dickens gives us the facts of Nemo's small kindness with that distancing phrase: "That graceless creature only knows."
The narrator is ventriloquising the contempt of the court, the contempt of society — and then the words that follow demolish that contempt entirely.
The scene Dickens lays out — Nemo turning back to look at a shivering boy in a doorway — is so spare and so cold and so tender all at once.
And then Nemo speaks:
"Neither have I. Not one!" — and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
Two sentences. Five words. And a world of loneliness recognised and met.
What strikes me about that passage is the question Nemo keeps asking Jo afterward — whether he slept sound, how he bore cold and hunger, whether he ever wished to die.
These are not the questions of charity. They're the questions of someone who knows the answers from the inside.
Nemo is not distributing benevolence downward. He recognises Jo as an equal in suffering.
The line — "I am as poor as you to-day, Jo" — is the one moment in the novel where a person of even marginal status addresses this invisible boy by name and as a peer.
The system produces these two figures — the destitute anonymous man and the destitute anonymous boy — and the only solidarity available to them is the solidarity of shared nothing.
I want to hold on to that detail about Jo giving his evidence — because the inquest then dismisses it.
A crossing-sweeper's testimony was worth almost nothing as formal evidence in this period.
Children of Jo's class were routinely found incompetent to testify — they were assumed not to understand the oath, not to grasp the meaning of truth under legal obligation.
And yet what Jo says — "He wos wery good to me, he wos!" — is the only true, the only human testimony in the entire proceeding.
The law cannot hear him. That is Dickens's indictment — rendered as a weeping child wiping his eyes with a wretched sleeve.
And then — after all the noise of the inquest — Dickens gives us that silent scene at the cemetery gate.
Jo comes back at night. He stands at the iron gate and looks in between the bars.
Dickens calls him "a slouching figure" — not even a boy, not a person, just a figure in the dark.
And then he does something utterly unexpected:
"It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and makes the archway clean."
That word "softly" — it kills me every time.
He has nothing. He can give nothing. And so he sweeps.
The pronoun is the thing that undoes me in that passage.
Dickens calls Jo "it" — "it holds the gate," "it then sweeps."
Some readers find that dehumanising. I read it as the opposite — as Dickens showing us what the world has made of this boy.
The society that cannot give Jo a name, a home, a friend, a legal voice — that society has produced an "it."
The indictment is in the grammar.
That's a formulation I want to sit with — the indictment in the grammar.
Because the very next chapter offers us another kind of grammar entirely — the grammar of power, of men who name everything and see nothing.
Lord Boodle's speech to Sir Leicester Dedlock in Chapter Twelve is one of Dickens's most sustained satirical performances, and it works by pure accumulation.
Coodle, Doodle, Foodle, Goodle, Hoodle — the rhyming nonsense names are the joke, but they're also the point.
These men are interchangeable. Their names have no content. Their offices have no purpose beyond their own perpetuation.
And then Dickens delivers the punchline with perfect gravity:
"What follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces (as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock) because you can't provide for Noodle!"
The country — shipwrecked — because Noodle hasn't been given a sinecure.
And Sir Leicester believes every word of it, which is what makes the satire so precise — the absurdity is entirely invisible to its participants.
The structural cruelty of placing this scene so close to Jo's chapter is Dickens at his most deliberate.
We have just watched a boy weep over a man that the law refused to see, who could not testify, who swept a step in the dark as an act of love.
And now we are in a drawing room where men of enormous power worry about whether Noodle can be accommodated.
The system has infinite ingenuity for taking care of its own. It has none for taking care of Jo.
There's also something formally brilliant about the Boodle passage — the way it mimics political speech.
It has all the scaffolding of serious argument: "He perceives with astonishment," "in consequence of the breach arising out of that affair" — the whole apparatus of statesmanlike reasoning.
Applied entirely to the question of where to put Noodle.

And the narrator's parenthetical — "as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock" — that little needle-prick tells you that the system's greatest achievement is making its own absurdity feel like gravity.
A world of infinite names for power, and a boy who is called "it."
Dickens holds both of those truths in this novel simultaneously, and the tension between them is the engine of everything.
Thank you, Daniel, James, and Caroline — this has been, as always, exactly the conversation this novel demands.
We'll be back next time to follow the fog further.

segments.title: A Secret Locked Away: Lady Dedlock's Hidden Life

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been tracking the novel's great fog — legal, moral, social — and today we turn to something more intimate and more devastating.
Lady Dedlock's secret — and the long, slow revelation of what it means.
With me to unpack it: Dr. Daniel Rosen, cultural historian, who reads every great house as a machine for concealment.
Professor James Blackstone, legal historian, who knows exactly what the law was doing — and to whom — in mid-Victorian England.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who has been moved by Esther Summerson's chapters since she was a teenager.
Let's begin with the lawyer at the centre of it all: Mr. Tulkinghorn.
Tulkinghorn is one of Dickens's most original creations — and one of the most frightening.
He's a solicitor in the old sense: a man who holds other people's affairs.
But Dickens gives us something the legal record never could.
The description of him walking toward the Dedlocks on the terrace is, I think, one of the great character portraits in the novel.
Dickens writes:
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
"He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself."
That final phrase — he is his own client — is legally precise and morally chilling in equal measure.
He has placed himself outside the systems of accountability that theoretically govern everyone else.
What's so important about that passage is the pace — the gait.
"His usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never slackened."
That's not a man hurrying to serve — that's a man who knows the power belongs to him.
The aristocracy pays his bills, but he holds their secrets.
And in Dickens's world, the person who holds the secret holds the real power — regardless of rank or title.
Lady Dedlock is presented to us as the apex of social grandeur — and yet she is already this man's hostage.
And what I find devastating is how Dickens shows the trap closing — from inside the room, in real time.
There's that scene where Sir Leicester reads out Tulkinghorn's letter — and he takes absolutely ages over it.
He fumbles with his eye-glass, loses his place, apologises.
And then finally he finds it and reads:
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity.
I have seen him."
Three words at the end.
And they fall into the room like stones into water.
Lady Dedlock says nothing — she has to say nothing — and yet Dickens makes us feel precisely what those three words cost her.
And the narrative makes the mutual watching explicit — almost clinical.
While Sir Leicester stares at the fire — unseeing, uncomprehending — the other two are locked in a silent contest.
Dickens writes — and this is extraordinary — that they have looked very steadily at one another throughout.
"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares;
what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
Hidden, for the time — that qualifying phrase does an enormous amount of work.
Dickens is telling us that this concealment will not hold — that its unravelling is already written into the structure of the novel.
And Sir Leicester is beautifully placed in that scene — staring at the fire with, as Dickens puts it, the expression of the Dedlock on the staircase.
He is, in that moment, already a portrait.
He has become his own ancestral painting — decorative, sightless, and entirely irrelevant to the real business being conducted in the room.
The aristocracy in this novel exists to be looked through — not at.
The actual power sits elsewhere: in Tulkinghorn's creased black suit.
And then there's the moment when the secret reaches across generations — when Esther meets Lady Dedlock's gaze.
Caroline, this is your territory — the reading experience itself.
It's the scene I return to most often in the novel.
Esther is narrating it retrospectively — she already knows, as she writes, what that look meant.
But she withholds that knowledge from us, and instead gives us only the sensation.
She asks:
"Shall I ever forget the rapid beating at my heart, occasioned by the look I met as I stood up!
Shall I ever forget the manner in which those handsome proud eyes seemed to spring out of their languor and to hold mine!"
Spring out of their languor — that verb is doing everything.
Lady Dedlock is famous for her boredom, her impenetrable composure.
And in one involuntary instant, that mask slips — and only Esther sees it.
What strikes me is the class geometry of that moment.
Esther is the illegitimate child — socially invisible, practically without origin.
Lady Dedlock is the apex of fashionable society.
And what Dickens insists upon — insists — is that the body knows what the social order has erased.
Esther writes of something quickened within her — her words — associated with the lonely days of her childhood.

"Very strangely, there was something quickened within me, associated with the lonely days at my godmother's; yes, away even to the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little glass after dressing my doll."
That image — dressing the doll, standing on tiptoe — is Dickens at his most precise.
Esther's earliest self is conjured up by the sight of her mother — whom she does not know is her mother.
And she works so hard to explain it away — that's what I find unbearable on re-reading.
She considers whether Lady Dedlock's face resembles her godmother's — and rules it out, carefully and correctly.
She is absolutely certain they have never met.
And then she is left with only the feeling — with no explanation that fits — and she gives us this:
"And yet I — I, little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on whose birthday there was no rejoicing — seemed to arise before my own eyes,
evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady, whom I not only entertained no fancy that I had ever seen, but whom I perfectly well knew I had never seen until that hour."
That dash after the first 'I' — 'And yet I — I' — she has to say her own name twice, as though to hold herself together.
And on whose birthday there was no rejoicing.
Every time I reach that clause, I have to put the book down.
What Dickens has done, architecturally, is to run two parallel secrets through the same narrative machinery.
There is Tulkinghorn's knowledge — external, predatory, legal in form if not in spirit.
And there is Esther's recognition — internal, instinctual, completely outside the law's comprehension.
The law tracks Lady Dedlock's secret through documents — the handwriting on an affidavit.
The body tracks it through something the law has no language for at all.
The law closes in from one direction; blood calls from another.
And Lady Dedlock stands between them — composed, watched, and entirely alone.
We'll take a short break — and when we return, we'll follow the thread of that handwriting all the way to its source.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're looking at one of the novel's quieter tragedies — the slow unraveling of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins Bleak House as a charming, energetic young man full of promise.
And Dickens disassembles him, carefully and without melodrama, across hundreds of pages.
With me today are three guests who each bring something distinct to this conversation.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomies of class power — and he'll show us how Richard's ruin is not merely personal but structural.
Prof. James Blackstone brings the legal and social history — what Chancery actually was, and what it did to the people caught inside it.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is here as our close reader — the person who catches what's happening in the sentences themselves.
Let's begin at the beginning of Richard's story — or rather, at its hinge point, that early conversation in chapter thirteen where Mr. Jarndyce speaks to Richard and Ada about their love.
What strikes me first about that chapter is how Esther frames the scene before anyone says a word.
Richard and Ada bring a chair to either side of her — she's literally placed between them.
And Esther says something rather beautiful about what follows.
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
That parenthetical — "I enjoyed it too much myself" — is Esther at her most honest.
She's enchanted by them, just as we are.
And that makes what's coming so much harder to bear.
But look at what she says immediately after that delight — the qualification that follows.
The happiness of that early love "could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty."
Constancy, fortitude, perseverance — each for the other's sake.
These are the virtues that Richard will be systematically unable to sustain.
And Dickens plants the diagnosis right here, in the tenderness of the opening scene.
That's precisely right, and Jarndyce sees it too — which is what makes his speech to Richard so remarkable.
He doesn't moralize or lecture in the usual Victorian guardian mode.
He states a principle with the clarity of someone who has watched young men fail before.
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
That image — the heathen waggoner who prays but won't put his shoulder to the wheel — is bracingly irreverent coming from a Victorian patriarch.
But the real thrust is in what follows — Jarndyce's warning about fits and starts.

"If you entertain the supposition that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here."
That last clause — leave your cousin Ada here — is not gentle. It's an ultimatum dressed as counsel.
And Richard essentially says — yes, absolutely, I will work my fingers to the bone.
And he means it, in that moment. That's the tragedy — he's not cynical.
But then there's that passage at the end of the chapter which I find almost unbearably beautiful.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
Dickens lets you have that radiance fully for exactly one sentence.
And then: "So they passed away into the shadow and were gone."
"It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
The room darkens. Esther registers it. And we know.
That Gothic weather — the sun clouding over precisely as they leave — is doing serious ideological work.
The novel is naturalizing what is actually a social and institutional process.
Richard isn't destroyed by fate. He is destroyed by Chancery.
The clouded sun is beautiful writing, but it risks making Richard's destruction look like weather — like something that just happens.
Dickens knows better than that, I think. But the Gothic imagery sometimes obscures the argument the novel is making.
I'd push back slightly there — or at least add a layer.
What the novel is also tracking is character — specifically, the absence of vocation.
When Richard fails at medicine, Mrs. Badger puts it with surgical precision.
"He has not that positive interest in it which makes it his vocation. If he has any decided impression in reference to it, I should say it was that it is a tiresome pursuit."
And she immediately contrasts Richard with Woodcourt — a young man who chose medicine from something real inside himself.

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
Richard has no such anchor. And without it, Chancery is not merely a distraction — it becomes the only story he can tell himself.
That's fair — and the contrast with Woodcourt is pointed.
But I'd ask: where does Richard's restlessness come from in the first place?
He's an orphan, a ward of Chancery, a young man whose entire future has been held in suspension by a legal process since before he was conscious of it.
Jarndyce tells him to trust Providence and his own efforts — but Richard has grown up inside a system that systematically undermines the very idea that effort leads to outcome.
Chancery has already taught him, at the cellular level, that the world runs on waiting and hoping and the arbitrary decisions of courts.
And Jarndyce sees all of that, which is why his earlier speech to Ada and Richard is so tender and so honest about its own limitations.
He explicitly says — I have no power over you whatever.
"I am only your friend and distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it."
That word — forfeit. Jarndyce is acutely aware that guardians can lose the trust they depend on.
He's speaking carefully around a catastrophe he can already see forming.
So we have the structure of the fall laid out in a single chapter — the hope, the warning, the foreshadowing, and the institutional trap already sprung before Richard walks into it.

That combination of personal character and systemic force — that tension between Jarndyce's counsel and what Chancery has already made of Richard — feels like the novel's central argument about how people unravel.
In our next segment, we'll look at how that unraveling accelerates — what Chancery's hold on Richard's imagination actually looks like in practice, and what it costs Ada.

segments.title: Dickens at Play: Humor and the Human Condition

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we sit with one of the great novels of the English language and try to understand why it still matters.
I'm joined today by three voices I trust enormously on this territory.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — every institution, every courtroom, every act of charity, a mechanism for keeping some people down.

Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows what the institutions Dickens satirised actually were — and can tell us whether Dickens was being fair, or whether the truth was even worse.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and brings us the experience of reading it — what makes you stop, re-read, laugh, grieve.
Today we're asking a question that sounds almost frivolous but turns out to be one of the deepest things you can ask about this novel.
How does Dickens make us laugh — and what is that laughter doing?
The first thing to say is that the comedy in Bleak House is never innocent.
It's always doing several things at once — entertaining you, yes, but also showing you something you might prefer not to see.
There's a passage early on that I find almost unbearable — and yet it's written with this extraordinary deadpan comedy.
Esther and Ada and Richard have just met this strange old woman in the court of Chancery.
Richard calls her mad, and she turns on him with terrifying precision.
She says:
"I was a ward myself. I was not mad at that time. I had youth and hope. I believe, beauty. It matters very little now."
And then she delivers the line that just stops my heart every single time.
"Neither of the three served or saved me. I have the honour to attend court regularly. With my documents. I expect a judgment. Shortly. On the Day of Judgment."
Those single-sentence fragments — that staccato rhythm — it's like watching a mind that has been broken into pieces by the court, and the pieces have arranged themselves into a terrible logic.
What Caroline is pointing to is that Dickens understands something most satirists miss.
The system doesn't break people randomly. It breaks them in the shape of the system.
That woman's speech mimics Chancery procedure — the short declarative notices, the expectation of judgment, the endless deferral.
She has internalised the court so completely that her madness is the court speaking through her.
And crucially — she's not wrong. She's just applying the court's logic to the only tribunal that might actually deliver.
The historical detail there is worth dwelling on.
Chancery wards were real — children whose estates were administered by the court, sometimes for decades, sometimes for their entire adult lives.
There were documented cases of individuals who became, quite literally, wards for life — perpetual litigants, slowly consumed by hope deferred.
So when she says 'I expect a judgment. Shortly' — and then adds 'On the Day of Judgment' — Dickens is making a theological joke, yes, but it's grounded in a very precise institutional reality.
The only difference between Chancery and eternity is that eternity is, at least, eventual.
That line should be on a plaque somewhere.
But I want to turn to a very different kind of comedy, because Dickens operates across such a range.
Mr. Vholes is one of the great comic monsters of English fiction — and yet he's funny in a way that is almost entirely achieved through restraint.
He's asked, in effect, whether Ada is beautiful.
And he says:
"As to beauty, I am not a judge of that myself, and I never did give much attention to it from a boy."
And then — magnificently — he outsources even that modest assessment:
"I dare say the young lady is equally eligible in that point of view. She is considered so (I have heard) among the clerks in the Inn, and it is a point more in their way than in mine."
He can't even concede beauty without a disclaimer. He's heard about it. Second-hand. From junior clerks.
Vholes is doing something that goes beyond being funny, though.
Every time he speaks, he performs a kind of moral laundering — wrapping predation in the language of professional duty.
He's stripping Richard of his inheritance while repeatedly invoking his 'duty to Mr. C.'s connexions.'
The comedy is the gap between that language and what is actually happening.
And Dickens knows that that gap is not just Vholes — it's the whole professional class.
The solicitor's language there is extraordinarily accurate to the period.
'Connexions' is a precise legal term — the people a solicitor was professionally obligated to consider, distinct from his actual client.
What Dickens has done is take that legitimate term and show how it can be weaponised — how the language of duty becomes the instrument of exploitation.
And the joke about beauty is funnier when you know that Vholes is simultaneously assessing Ada's value as collateral for Richard's ongoing litigation.
And then there is Mr. Bucket — who is a comedian of an entirely different order.
Bucket is funny in the way a great detective is funny — he knows more than he's saying, and he enjoys knowing it.
There's a scene with old Smallweed where Bucket is extracting information, and he does it with this extraordinary air of jovial conspiracy.
He steers Smallweed toward admitting he found a document, saying:
"And so you chance to find, you know, a paper with the signature of Jarndyce to it. Don't you?"
'Don't you?' — the question is doing all the work. It's not really a question at all.
And then — having manoeuvred Smallweed into position — he reveals what the paper is.
"What do you find it to be but a will, you see. That's the drollery of it."
'That's the drollery of it.' He's laughing at his own joke. And it is funny. And it's also the most consequential document in the entire novel.
Bucket is the novel's most sophisticated ideological operator.
His charm is a professional instrument — it disarms, it implicates, it makes the person being manipulated feel like a collaborator.
'Cheerful raillery' is Esther's phrase for what he's doing to Smallweed — and it's perfect, because Smallweed 'by no means reciprocated' it.
The humour is entirely one-directional. Bucket finds himself delightful. Smallweed is merely trapped.
It's worth noting that a will turning up at that stage of the narrative is precisely the kind of thing that actually happened in protracted Chancery cases.
Documents were suppressed, mislaid, discovered decades late — sometimes by people who had every reason to keep them hidden.
Dickens calls it 'the drollery of it' — and the historical record suggests that the real cases were, if anything, more darkly absurd than the fiction.
Which raises the uncomfortable question of whether Dickens was satirising the system, or whether the system was simply providing him with material.
That question — whether the comedy illuminates the system or merely aestheticises it — feels like exactly the right place to pause.
What we've seen today is that Dickens's humour is never decorative.
It's structural — it's doing the same work as the tragedy, sometimes in the same sentence.
My thanks to Caroline Woodcourt, Daniel Rosen, and James Blackstone for a conversation that has made me want to go back and re-read every page.
We'll be back with more Bleak House Unpacked very soon.

segments.title: Narrative Entanglements: How Dickens Weaves His Web

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and with full appreciation of its magnificent complexity.
I'm your host, and today we're examining how Dickens constructs his narrative web — secrets buried inside other secrets, identity withheld, watchers watching other watchers.
With me are three readers who know this novel as well as anyone.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in the novel as a machine for protecting power — and every secret as a symptom of that machine.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he brings the real-world context of what these institutions actually were, and what it meant to live inside them.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong re-reader of Bleak House, attentive to the verbal music and deeply invested in the characters' fates.
Let's begin with the architecture of concealment that runs through this novel — and two figures who embody it perfectly: Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn.
What strikes me every time I return to Chesney Wold is how Dickens stages the scenes between Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn as a kind of silent theatre.
They are always in the same rooms, performing the same social rituals — and absolutely nothing is said between them that could be called dangerous.
And yet the passage radiates menace.
Listen to how Dickens describes their mutual surveillance — this is his best quote in the passage, and I want to read it slowly.

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
That phrase — "never to be taken unawares" — that is a military phrase, isn't it.
These two are not at a country-house dinner; they are at war.
Caroline is right that it's war — but we should be precise about what kind of war.
Tulkinghorn holds information about Lady Dedlock that could destroy her social position entirely.
And what is Lady Dedlock's social position, finally?
It is the property of Sir Leicester Dedlock — his name, his rank, his ancient lineage made flesh and placed on display.
Dickens gives us that extraordinary image: she is an "exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
The religious vocabulary is not incidental — Lady Dedlock is a figure of worship, but the worship is purely social, and it is killing her.
Tulkinghorn, meanwhile, is "the speechless repository of noble confidences" — he holds the secrets of the ruling class, and that makes him their most dangerous servant.
Daniel's point about Tulkinghorn is historically exact, and worth pressing further.
A family solicitor of this period was not merely a legal functionary — he was the custodian of every embarrassing document, every entailed debt, every inconvenient birth.
The phrase Dickens uses — "oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home" — captures something sociologically precise about such men.
They were not of the aristocracy and never would be; but the aristocracy could not function without them.
Which meant the power ran in unexpected directions — and Dickens understood that perfectly.
That tension between surface and concealment runs not only through the Chesney Wold scenes — it structures the revelation about Esther's origins as well.
Mr. Jarndyce's account of the letter he received is one of the most quietly devastating passages in the novel.
I find this section almost unbearable to read, and I've read it many times.
Jarndyce is telling Esther — in the gentlest possible terms — the story of her own abandonment.
The letter he received was, in his words, "written with a stern passion and power that rendered it unlike all other letters I have ever read."
That is Lady Dedlock's voice reaching us through Jarndyce — and Dickens denies us the letter itself.
We only ever get the report of it, mediated twice over.
The woman who wrote it — with such feeling, such force — has made herself deliberately inaccessible.
What that letter contains is the evidence of illegitimacy — and illegitimacy in this period was not a private sorrow but a legal and economic catastrophe.
Jarndyce reads from it — tells Esther that the writer had "bred her in secrecy from her birth, had blotted out all trace of her existence."
"Blotted out" — that is a phrase of extraordinary violence.
A child is reduced to a problem of documentation — to ink on a page that must be made not to exist.
And then — and this is where Dickens's radicalism surfaces — the letter frames this erasure as moral necessity.
Jarndyce tells Esther of "the distorted religion which clouded her mind with impressions of the need there was for the child to expiate an offence of which she was quite innocent."
The child must suffer so that the mother's sin — the social construction of sin — can be managed.
The word "distorted" is Jarndyce's gloss — and it matters enormously that he applies it.
Because this was not, in Victorian England, a fringe theological position — it was the mainstream view of illegitimate children.
The child carried the moral taint of the parent's transgression, full stop.
What Dickens does — through Jarndyce's word "distorted" — is quietly declare the entire framework corrupt.

And the legal dimension of the secret is equally severe: the passage makes clear that the lady giving instructions to Mr. Kenge had resolved, as Jarndyce puts it, that "more than this she would never for any human consideration disclose."
"That more than this she would never (and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution) for any human consideration disclose."
The parenthesis — "he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution" — is lawyerly and chilling at once.
And the name she gives Kenge — an assumed one.
She tells him of her own accord: the name is not real.
Which means the only thing she volunteers is the admission of a fiction.
The real identity — Lady Dedlock, the woman sitting at Chesney Wold being watched by Tulkinghorn — remains absolutely hidden.
And Esther is left to be, in the writer's own admission, "entirely friendless, nameless, and unknown."
Three words. Each one worse than the last.
What emerges from all of this is the sense that the novel's plot is itself a kind of entanglement — secrets generating more secrets, identities concealed inside concealed identities.
Lady Dedlock watches Tulkinghorn; Tulkinghorn watches Lady Dedlock; Jarndyce guards a secret from Esther; Esther does not yet know whose secret it is.
In our next segment, we'll follow what happens when that web begins — very slowly, very inexorably — to pull tight.
We've spent this episode moving through Bleak House's great machinery — the courts, the slums, the drawing rooms.
And what I want to close with is the weight of it — what Dickens leaves us holding when the last page turns.
Three images keep returning to me from what we've discussed today: Vholes, Tulkinghorn, and Jo.
James, I'd like to start with you — because you've been sitting with two passages that seem to bookend the novel's relationship to institutions.
Yes, and what strikes me is how perfectly Dickens dramatises the mechanism by which reform is strangled at birth.
The Vholes passage isn't just satire — it's a transcript of how institutional self-preservation actually works.
Kenge doesn't defend the law on its merits — he can't, because it has none.
Instead, he makes the practitioner the argument.
Listen to the logic Dickens gives him — and it's worth reading in full, because every clause is a small act of violence.
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
And that is enough — that single invocation of Vholes — to kill a reform inquiry for a decade.
What James is describing is the ideological laundering of exploitation through the language of respectability.
Vholes is never actually present in that exchange — he functions as a symbol.
The system protects itself by humanising its worst instruments.
Give the predator a family to feed, a respectable name, and suddenly abolition becomes cruelty.
And then Dickens cuts, with extraordinary nerve, to the other end of the social scale — to Jo.
Where Vholes is defended by the entire machinery of parliamentary evidence, Jo is rejected even as a witness.
He cannot speak in any court that matters.
And yet — and this is why I keep coming back to this passage — Dickens refuses to let that be the final word on Jo.
The narrator addresses him directly: 'Jo, is it thou?'
That's not reportage — that's an act of tenderness.
And then comes the line that I find almost unbearable in its simplicity.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
Jo's entire moral life is contained in that sentence — misspelled, ungrammatical, and absolutely luminous.
The law cannot hear him, but gratitude is a kind of grace he possesses that Vholes never could.
That contrast becomes even more charged when you place it alongside the Tulkinghorn passage.
Tulkinghorn is the system's most perfected instrument — he holds everyone's secrets and releases none of them except for leverage.
And yet Dickens reminds us, in that late-night passage, that even Tulkinghorn is mortal — that the stars are watching him too.
The prose suddenly asks something extraordinary — almost metaphysical.
"Where are the digger and the spade, this peaceful night, destined to add the last great secret to the many secrets of the Tulkinghorn existence?"
The novel knows he will be murdered before he does.
And there's something deeply satisfying — even darkly comic — about the fact that the man who hoarded secrets ends as merely another one.
What I take from all three passages is that Dickens understands something most novelists flinch from.
The system doesn't fail by accident — it functions exactly as designed.
Vholes is protected, Jo is silenced, Tulkinghorn accumulates power until a force outside the system ends him.
Nothing is reformed from within — it has to be blown apart, or it simply grinds on.
And Dickens knew that — even if he couldn't quite bring himself to say it plainly.
I think that's right — and it's also why the novel doesn't end with triumph.
The court case outlasts almost everyone touched by it.
The question the novel keeps asking — in Jo's broken grammar, in those watching stars — is: who gets to be counted?
And the novel's answer is tender and furious at once.
Tender and furious — I can't think of a better description of Bleak House as a whole.
What this episode has confirmed, for me, is that Dickens built something that repays every re-reading.
Not because it gives us answers, but because it refuses to let us look away from the questions.
My thanks to Daniel Rosen, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt — who have each, today, given Bleak House exactly the kind of reading it deserves.
We'll be back next time with more from the archive of great English fiction.
Until then — keep reading.

c1:p0.text:
London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.
c1:p0.best_quote: As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.

c24:p154.text:
The sun was down, the light had gradually stolen from the roof, and
the shadow had crept upward. But to me the shadow of that pair, one
living and one dead, fell heavier on Richard’s departure than the
darkness of the darkest night. And through Richard’s farewell words I
heard it echoed: “Of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits
and hopes, of all the living and the dead world, this one poor soul
alone comes natural to me, and I am fit for. There is a tie of many
suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on
earth that Chancery has not broken!”
c24:p154.summary: Esther reflects on Gridley's final words, which echo through her memory and Richard's departure, reinforcing the novel's commentary on Chancery's destructive power.
c24:p154.best_quote: Of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits and hopes, of all the living and the dead world, this one poor soul alone comes natural to me, and I am fit for. There is a tie of many suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on earth that Chancery has not broken!

c58:p67.text:
“Therefore I desire to say, and to call you all to

of complaint against her. That I have ever had the strongest

c11:p74.text:

c11:p87.text:
That graceless creature only knows that the dead man (whom he
recognized just now by his yellow face and black hair) was sometimes
hooted and pursued about the streets. That one cold winter night when
he, the boy, was shivering in a doorway near his crossing, the man
turned to look at him, and came back, and having questioned him and
found that he had not a friend in the world, said, “Neither have I.
Not one!” and gave him the price of a supper and a night’s lodging.
That the man had often spoken to him since and asked him whether he
slept sound at night, and how he bore cold and hunger, and whether he
ever wished to die, and similar strange questions. That when the man
had no money, he would say in passing, “I am as poor as you to-day,
Jo,” but that when he had any, he had always (as the boy most
heartily believes) been glad to give him some.
c11:p87.summary: Jo reveals the dead man recognized him, showed him kindness, asked about his welfare, and when poor himself, shared what little he had.
c11:p87.best_quote: Neither have I. Not one! and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.

c11:p88.text:
“He was wery good to me,” says the boy, wiping his eyes with his
wretched sleeve. “Wen I see him a-layin’ so stritched out just now, I
wished he could have heerd me tell him so. He wos wery good to me, he
wos!”
c11:p88.summary: Jo weeps while expressing his gratitude and affection for the dead man.
c11:p88.best_quote: He wos wery good to me, he wos!

c11:p98.text:
With the night comes a slouching figure through the tunnel-court to
the outside of the iron gate. It holds the gate with its hands and
looks in between the bars, stands looking in for a little while.
c11:p98.summary: A slouching figure (Jo) comes through the tunnel-court to the cemetery gate and looks in.

c11:p99.text:
It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and
makes the archway clean. It does so very busily and trimly, looks in
again a little while, and so departs.
c11:p99.summary: Jo methodically sweeps the cemetery step and archway clean with his broom in quiet devotion.
c11:p99.best_quote: It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and makes the archway clean.

c12:p56.text:
Then there is my Lord Boodle, of considerable reputation with his
party, who has known what office is and who tells Sir Leicester
Dedlock with much gravity, after dinner, that he really does not see
to what the present age is tending. A debate is not what a debate
used to be; the House is not what the House used to be; even a
Cabinet is not what it formerly was. He perceives with astonishment
that supposing the present government to be overthrown, the limited
choice of the Crown, in the formation of a new ministry, would lie
between Lord Coodle and Sir Thomas Doodle—supposing it to be
impossible for the Duke of Foodle to act with Goodle, which may be
assumed to be the case in consequence of the breach arising out of
that affair with Hoodle. Then, giving the Home Department and the
leadership of the House of Commons to Joodle, the Exchequer to
Koodle, the Colonies to Loodle, and the Foreign Office to Moodle,
what are you to do with Noodle? You can’t offer him the Presidency of
the Council; that is reserved for Poodle. You can’t put him in the
Woods and Forests; that is hardly good enough for Quoodle. What
follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces
(as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock)
because you can’t provide for Noodle!
c12:p56.summary: Lord Boodle explains to Sir Leicester that government is failing because there is no office suitable for Noodle after all the important positions are distributed among his equally mediocre associates.
c12:p56.best_quote: What follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces (as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock) because you can't provide for Noodle!

c12:p67.text:
At length, one afternoon a little before sunset, when the bright
groups of figures which have for the last hour or two enlivened the
Ghost’s Walk are all dispersed and only Sir Leicester and my Lady
remain upon the terrace, Mr. Tulkinghorn appears. He comes towards
them at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never
slackened. He wears his usual expressionless mask—if it be a
mask—and carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every
crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great
or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his
personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients;
he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.
c12:p67.summary: At sunset, Tulkinghorn finally appears, moving at his usual methodical pace with an expressionless mask, embodying mystery and unknown knowledge.
c12:p67.best_quote: He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.

c12:p11.text:
“He sends—I really beg your pardon—he sends,” says Sir Leicester,
selecting the letter and unfolding it, “a message to you. Our
stopping to change horses as I came to his postscript drove it out of
my memory. I beg you’ll excuse me. He
 says—”  Sir Leicester is so
long in taking out his eye-glass and adjusting it that my Lady looks
a little irritated. “He says ‘In the matter of the right of way—’ I
beg your pardon, that’s not the place. He says—yes! Here I have it!
He says, ‘I beg my respectful compliments to my Lady, who, I hope,
has benefited by the change. Will you do me the favour to mention (as
it may interest her) that I have something to tell her on her return
in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery
suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen
him.’”
c12:p11.summary: Sir Leicester slowly reads Mr. Tulkinghorn's message stating that he has discovered the identity and location of the man who copied the affidavit Lady Dedlock inquired about.
c12:p11.best_quote: I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him.

c12:p114.text:
During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady
Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their
customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another—as
was natural, perhaps, in the discussion of so unusual a subject. Sir
Leicester has looked at the fire, with the general expression of the
Dedlock on the staircase. The story being told, he renews his stately
protest, saying that as it is quite clear that no association in my
Lady’s mind can possibly be traceable to this poor wretch (unless he
was a begging-letter writer), he trusts to hear no more about a
subject so far removed from my Lady’s station.
c12:p114.summary: Throughout the exchange, Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn watch each other intently while maintaining composure; Sir Leicester watches the fire. The narrative reveals their mutual suspicion and hidden knowledge.
c12:p114.best_quote: During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another—as was natural, perhaps, in the discussion of so unusual a subject...But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.

c18:p41.text:
Shall I ever forget the rapid beating at my heart, occasioned by the
look I met as I stood up! Shall I ever forget the manner in which
those handsome proud eyes seemed to spring out of their languor and
to hold mine! It was only a moment before I cast mine down—released
again, if I may say so—on my book; but I knew the beautiful face
quite well in that short space of time.
c18:p41.summary: Esther meets Lady Dedlock's eyes and experiences an overwhelming, inexplicable emotional shock that deeply disturbs her.
c18:p41.best_quote: "Shall I ever forget the rapid beating at my heart, occasioned by the look I met as I stood up! Shall I ever forget the manner in which those handsome proud eyes seemed to spring out of their languor and to hold mine!"

c18:p42.text:
And, very strangely, there was something quickened within me,
associated with the lonely days at my godmother’s; yes, away even to
the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little
glass after dressing my doll. And this, although I had never seen
this lady’s face before in all my life—I was quite sure of
it—absolutely certain.
c18:p42.summary: Esther experiences a strange association between Lady Dedlock and her childhood memories, though she is certain they have never met.
c18:p42.best_quote: "And, very strangely, there was something quickened within me, associated with the lonely days at my godmother's; yes, away even to the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little glass after dressing my doll."

c18:p44.text:
I felt it to be an unmeaning weakness in me and tried to overcome it
by attending to the words I heard. Then, very strangely, I seemed to
hear them, not in the reader’s voice, but in the well-remembered
voice of my godmother. This made me think, did Lady Dedlock’s face
accidentally resemble my godmother’s? It might be that it did, a
little; but the expression was so different, and the stern decision
which had worn into my godmother’s face, like weather into rocks, was
so completely wanting in the face before me that it could not be that
resemblance which had struck me. Neither did I know the loftiness and
haughtiness of Lady Dedlock’s face, at all, in any one. And yet I—I,
little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on
whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own
eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady,
whom I not only entertained no fancy that I had ever seen, but whom I
perfectly well knew I had never seen until that hour.
c18:p44.summary: Esther analyzes her emotional response, considering but rejecting a resemblance to her godmother, while feeling her entire past self summoned by something in Lady Dedlock.
c18:p44.best_quote: "And yet I—I, little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady, whom I not only entertained no fancy that I had ever seen, but whom I perfectly well knew I had never seen until that hour."

c13:p99.text:
There he was, of course. They brought a chair on either side of me,
and put me between them, and really seemed to have fallen in love
with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so
trustful, and so fond of me. They went on in their own wild way for a
little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said
that he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada said that
she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.
c13:p99.summary: Richard and Ada confide to Esther their mutual love, placing themselves on either side of her. Esther counsels them about the demands of enduring love and promises to speak to Mr. Jarndyce.
c13:p99.best_quote: They went on in their own wild way for a little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake.

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great

idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to
justify it. It told me of a child, an orphan girl then twelve years

consider if I would, in that case, finish what the writer had begun.”
